answer: The GTK buffer's `modified_changed` signal doesn't emit when undo/redo operations occur—this is expected GTK behavior. Undo bypasses the normal edit path. Solution: Connect to the `changed` signal instead, which fires on all modifications including undo. Alternatively, manually track undo/redo stack changes by connecting to the `undo_action_name` and `redo_action_name` properties if available, or wrap your text buffer to intercept undo/redo and manually emit notifications. For your use case, switching to `changed` is simplest: `text_view.get_buffer().connect('changed', on_modified_changed)`.

This is a macOS tkinter rendering bug where `grid_remove()` doesn't properly refresh the display on subsequent calls. The window manager retains stale geometry. Fix: Call `update_idletasks()` after `grid()` to force a redraw: `current_page.grid_remove()` → `new_page.grid()` → `window.update_idletasks()`. Alternatively, switch to `pack()`/`pack_forget()` which handles macOS refresh better. Or force a full window redraw with `window.update()` after switching. This is a known macOS/tkinter compatibility issue with no clean root cause fix.

This error indicates the transformers package exists but the Jupyter kernel isn't using it, likely due to kernel isolation. Verify the kernel has transformers: in Jupyter, run `!pip list | grep transformers`. If missing, install: `!pip install --upgrade transformers torch`. If already installed, the kernel may be pointing to a different Python. Restart the kernel after install. If using a conda environment, ensure it's the active environment when starting Jupyter. The M4 Mac isn't the issue—verify with `!which python` to confirm kernel Python matches your transformers installation.

Measuring latency across process boundaries with `time.perf_counter_ns()` is unreliable—each process has its own clock baseline. For GPU tensors, use `torch.cuda.Event` for GPU-side timing: synchronize on both producer and consumer with `torch.cuda.synchronize()`, then create events before/after transfers. For CPU timing, use a shared reference point via IPC or measure end-to-end in one process. Alternatively, use `time.time()` (lower resolution) consistently across both processes, acknowledging IPC jitter makes sub-millisecond precision unrealistic.

Use `list.eval()` with a conditional inside a map to replace and expand: `df.with_columns(pl.col('a').map_elements(lambda lst: [x if x != '55' else '55.11,55.12' for x in lst]).str.split(',').list.explode()).drop('a').rename({'a': 'a'})`. Better: use `list.eval()` directly: `df.with_columns(pl.col('a').list.eval(pl.when(pl.element() == '55').then(pl.lit(['55.11', '55.12'])).otherwise(pl.lit([pl.element()]))).list.explode())`.

Your regex `\w*\d\w*` removes all words containing digits, killing dates and 'No'. Remove that line entirely. Instead, selectively clean only the 'Name' column: apply lowercasing and punctuation removal to specific columns, not globally. Stopwords removes 'No'—exclude 'status' column from stopword filtering. Better approach: clean each column separately with targeted regex: Name gets alphanumeric normalization, Date is left alone, Status/Number bypass cleaning. Use `df.loc[:, col] = df[col].apply(cleaning_func)` for column-specific operations.

Static arguments cannot be differentiated. `omega` is marked static, but `grad()` tries to trace through it. Solution: remove `omega` from `static_argnames` in the inner `hamiltonian` jit if you need gradients w.r.t. it. If `omega` must be static (e.g., JIT compilation depends on its value), don't differentiate w.r.t. it—only compute gradients for `kappa` and `alpha0`. Use `grad(solve_diff, argnums=(2, 3))` to exclude `omega` and `n`. Alternatively, restructure: don't nest jits; keep `hamiltonian` undecorated or make it a traced function.

Partial embeddings suggest ELSER inference timeout or pipeline processor failure. Check: (1) Task logs: `GET /_task/taskid?detailed` to see processor-level errors; (2) Verify ELSER model still deployed: `GET /_ml/trained_models`; (3) Retries consumed without error logging. Solution: Reindex with smaller batch size (100-200), add `timeout` to pipeline config, increase model resources. Check indices mapping for `rank_features` field configuration. Run a subset first: `size: 10` to confirm pipeline works end-to-end before full reindex.

Dynaconf's `@get` on nested lists returns intermediate dict structure instead of the final list. Workaround: (1) Add `dynaconf_merge = true` to the section containing `@get` reference; (2) Flatten the config path—use `@get google.calendar` instead of splitting; (3) Use a direct reference without nesting. Example: `[default.celery.google.calendar] ids = @get google.calendar.calendar_ids` instead of nested reference. This is a known limitation when `@get` references nested structures—flattening paths resolves it.

You're building strings, not DataFrames. Use pd.DataFrame with a list of dicts: `results = []; [results.append({'Lookup item': item, 'Corresponding item': get_score_by_id(df_past, item) or 'NAN'}) for item in items]; new_df = pd.DataFrame(results)`. Or more concisely: `new_df = pd.DataFrame({'Lookup item': items, 'Corresponding item': [get_score_by_id(df_past, i) or 'NAN' for i in items]})`. Avoid building strings with string concatenation—that won't parse back into a DataFrame.

You can't remove just the title bar on Windows without removing borders—`overrideredirect(True)` removes both. Alternatives: (1) Use `wm_attributes('-toolwindow', 1)` on Windows for a thinner title bar; (2) Accept the standard frame. On Linux/Mac, `overrideredirect()` offers more control. tkinter doesn't expose fine-grained window chrome control. If you need custom chrome, consider PyQt5/PySide2 which wraps native APIs for title bar customization.

Redis Stream consumer group 'taskiq' doesn't exist or expires after inactivity. On worker startup, the group isn't re-created. Solution: (1) Ensure the scheduler creates the group during startup with proper retention; (2) Configure Redis persistence: add consumer group config in taskiq broker setup. Check Redis: `XINFO STREAM taskiq` to verify group exists. (3) Handle the error gracefully with retry logic. Add initialization in broker setup: check/create group on first run.

Random 1-minute hangs with Gunicorn 2 workers × 4 threads (8 total) suggest thread pool exhaustion or database lock. If a callback blocks all threads (sync DB query, heavy compute), requests queue. Solutions: (1) Convert callbacks to async with `dcc.Loading` to prevent blocking; (2) Increase worker processes/threads; (3) Profile with py-spy to find blocking calls; (4) Add timeouts to DB queries. Check Gunicorn logs: `gunicorn --access-logfile - --error-logfile -`. The 800ms→60s jump indicates contention, not network latency.

Use a list comprehension for Pythonic filtering: `[k for k in d.keys() if k[0] == n]`. More readable than a loop. For iteration efficiency, omit `.keys()` since dict iteration is already keys: `[k for k in d if k[0] == n]`. For functional style: `filter(lambda k: k[0] == n, d)`. Dict comprehension variant: `{k: d[k] for k in d if k[0] == n}` if you need the values too. All are idiomatic Python 3.12.

Type checkers can't infer T from union/Annotated types at call-time. Use TypeVar with bound and @overload, but accept that special forms fall to `Any`: `from typing import TypeVar, Union; T = TypeVar('T'); def convert(value: Any, output_type: type[T] = Any) -> T: adapter = TypeAdapter(output_type); return adapter.validate_python(value)`. Pydantic's TypeAdapter handles runtime validation correctly; static type inference for `int | str` requires explicit type narrowing post-call or passing as `Literal` strings.

507 Insufficient Storage means the server rejected your request due to lack of resources. You're likely rate-limited or blocked; 507 differs from 429 (rate limit). Verify with a non-proxy request first. If consistent with proxies, either the proxy pool is exhausted or the site blocks rotating-proxies. Solutions: (1) Add request delays: `DOWNLOAD_DELAY = 2`; (2) Rotate user agents; (3) Check if proxy IPs are blocked; (4) Use single static proxy if available. 507 can also indicate server issues—try again later.

Set the y-axis lower bound explicitly: `plt.ylim(bottom=2)` before `MaxNLocator`. MaxNLocator respects manual limits. Alternatively, use explicit ticks: `plt.yticks(range(2, int(df['mag'].max()) + 1))`. Or with MaxNLocator: `ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(nbins=30, integer=True))` and set limits via `set_ylim(2, None)`.

StatefulDoFn's process() must yield elements, not return floats. The error 'float is not iterable' suggests `process()` returns a single float instead of an iterable. Solution: Ensure `process()` yields the EMA value: `yield (key, ema_value)`. Use `BagStateSpec` to store EMA state per key. Check your `process()` signature returns a generator or list. Example: `def process(self, element): ... state.write(new_ema) ... yield (element['key'], new_ema)` not `return ema_value`.
